name: The World of AI: Power and Cooling section on datacenter electricity
title: The World of AI: Power and Cooling section on datacenter electricity
answer: This is the Power and Cooling section of The World of AI, a curated atlas of AI infrastructure pages. It holds three entries on how an AI datacenter gets electricity and sheds heat, covering grid interconnection queues, contracted generation and the shift from air to liquid cooling. Its most useful single point is the demand figure it carries from the Department of Energy's 2024 LBNL report: datacenters used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver.

sections.body: It is a section index page on theworldofai.org, published by The World of AI, which describes itself as an atlas of artificial intelligence covering law, litigation and definitions, rebuilt daily from primary sources. This particular page is the Power and Cooling section, one part of the site's technology and core infrastructure area. It states that the section holds three entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily. The page carries a citation line dated 26 September 2026, which is the retrieval date given, and it also carries promotional material for the publisher's books and consulting audits. No publication date is given for the entries themselves.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: This is a section index page rather than an article. It states that Power and Cooling holds three entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily, and that the section covers how an AI datacenter gets electricity and gets rid of heat. The named topics are grid connection and interconnection queues, the generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling that dense GPU racks forced. It points readers elsewhere for individual facilities, which sit in Data Centers, and for racks and interconnect, which sit in other hardware sections. The substantive claim is a demand figure attributed to the Department of Energy's 2024 LBNL report: datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. The page reads this as a hard constraint on AI scaling, arguing the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows, so training and inference at scale will need new generation capacity, storage or load shifting, none of which are built yet. It also says the width of the 6.7 to 12% range signals uncertainty about how fast AI deployment happens, depending on factors the electricity numbers alone cannot capture.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page gives three entries in the Power and Cooling section. It attributes to the Department of Energy's 2024 LBNL report the figures of about 4.4% of US electricity consumed by datacenters in 2023 and a projection of 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI named as the driver. It states that the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows, and that new generation capacity, storage or load shifting would be needed and none are built yet. It says the width of the projection range signals uncertainty about the pace of AI deployment. The citation line gives a retrieval date of 26 September 2026.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in the energy industry, this page is useful mainly as a dated, citable pointer to the Department of Energy's 2024 LBNL demand figures, and as a short statement of the power constraint that sits behind datacenter siting, interconnection queues and cooling choices. It frames electricity supply as a limit on AI scaling rather than a background cost, and it names the three areas the site tracks: grid connection, contracted generation and the move to liquid cooling. Anyone building an argument about datacenter load growth, or looking for where that argument is tracked and re-verified, can use this page as the entry point, while treating the underlying numbers as coming from the DOE analysis rather than from the site itself.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: The page is a section landing page with little substance of its own. It lists three entries but does not reproduce them, so no vendor names, project details, regional breakdowns or methodology appear here. The demand figures are attributed to the Department of Energy's 2024 LBNL report, but the page does not explain how the 6.7 to 12% range was derived or what assumptions sit behind it. No dates are given for the individual entries, only a retrieval date for the page. The page is also partly commercial, carrying promotion for the publisher's books, a novel and a list of named audit and assessment services, which a reader should weigh when judging how independent the curation is.
